does-a-mobile-subscription-pay-me-less.h.text:
← Twitch payout calculator

Does a mobile subscription pay me less?

Apple and Google take roughly 30% of an in-app purchase, so it's a reasonable guess that a subscription bought in Twitch's iOS or Android app pays the streamer less than the same tier bought on the web. As of Twitch's October 2024 pricing change, that guess is wrong — and getting it right matters if you're deciding whether to steer viewers toward one platform or the other.

Open the free payout calculator

What Twitch actually does about the app store cut

Twitch charges more for a Tier 1 subscription bought in the mobile app (about $7.99 in the US) than for the same tier bought on the web (about $5.99). The gap exists specifically to cover the app store's cut, so that the amount left over for Twitch and the streamer to split is the same either way. Twitch has stated plainly that a streamer earns the same amount from a subscription whether it's desktop or mobile.

Twitch does not publish the exact intermediate accounting between the mobile price and the split, and this page does not invent one. What matters for your own math is the confirmed outcome, not the plumbing behind it:

FigureWeb subscriptionMobile (iOS/Android) subscription
Price the viewer pays (Tier 1, approx.)$5.99$7.99
Extra above the web price—~$2.00, sized to cover the app store's cut
Your payout at a 50% split$2.995$2.995

Same payout, same tier, different platform. So when you use the calculator, enter your subscriber counts by tier without worrying about which platform each one bought on — one Tier 1 sub is one Tier 1 sub for payout purposes.

What actually does change your payout

Your revenue split. Everyone starts at 50% of subscription revenue. Sustaining 100 Plus Points for three consecutive months moves you to 60% under Twitch's Plus Program, and 300 Plus Points moves you to 70%. Moving from 50% to 60% or 70% is a real, large change to what you keep on identical sub numbers — re-run the calculator at each split to see the size of that gap for your own month.

The tier itself. A Tier 2 sub pays roughly twice a Tier 1 sub before the split, and Tier 3 roughly five times — obvious once stated, but easy to lose track of when subs of different tiers are lumped into one "sub count" in your head.

Common questions

Does a mobile Twitch subscription pay the streamer less than a desktop one?

No. Since Twitch's October 2024 pricing change, a Tier 1 subscription costs more on the iOS or Android app (about $7.99) than on the web ($5.99) specifically so that the extra covers Apple's and Google's in-app-purchase fee before it ever reaches the revenue split. Twitch has stated that a streamer earns the same amount from a subscription whether it's bought on desktop or mobile.

So what actually changes how much I get paid per sub?

Two things: your revenue split (50% default, or 60%/70% under Twitch's Plus Program) and the subscription tier itself. Purchase platform is not one of them, as of the pricing change described above.

Does the same logic apply to Bits bought in the mobile app?

Bits are priced with Twitch's own margin already built into what a viewer pays for a Bits bundle, and a cheered Bit is worth a flat one cent to the streamer regardless of platform or split. This calculator treats Bits the same way whichever platform they were bought on.

Could this change again?

Yes. Twitch has changed subscription pricing and platform-fee handling before, and it publishes no live feed a static page could read. Treat this explainer as current as of the date on this page and verify anything material against your own Twitch dashboard and Twitch's own current help documentation.

FOR TWITCH STREAMERS

The dashboard number isn't your payout. Take-home is.

"$414 in sub revenue this month" is not what lands in your bank account — your revenue split (50% by default, or 60%/70% under the Plus Program) cuts subs, Bits pay a flat $0.01 each, and mobile subs pay exactly the same as desktop ones despite what the app store fee headlines suggest. This free calculator finds your real monthly take-home and checks it against an income goal.

Think buying on mobile pays you less? See does a mobile subscription pay me less? for the worked answer. Tracking this in a spreadsheet today instead? See this calculator vs. a spreadsheet.

Your month

Subs by tier

Include gifted subs in the tier they were gifted at — the giver pays, but your payout works the same as any other sub. Include mobile-purchased subs in the same counts too: your payout per sub is the same regardless of platform (see the linked explainer above).

Split & other income

50% is the default split. Sustaining 100 Plus Points for three consecutive months moves you to 60% under Twitch's Plus Program; 300 Plus Points moves you to 70%. Read yours off your own Twitch dashboard. "Other monthly income" is ads, sponsorships, or donations elsewhere — a figure you supply, since Twitch publishes no ad rate this tool could model honestly.

Your numbers above are saved locally in this browser so you don't retype them next time. A shareable link puts the same numbers in the URL fragment — nothing is uploaded.

This is a planning floor from the numbers you typed, not your actual payout statement. It does not model ad revenue, currency conversion, or any promotional rate — fold those into "other monthly income" yourself. It never reads your Twitch account or replaces your own payout dashboard.

Private by default

Everything on this page runs in your browser and nothing is ever uploaded. Your sub counts, prices, split, Bits, other income, and target payout are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them next time — Reset to defaults clears them, and Copy shareable link puts them in a URL fragment your browser never sends anywhere. There is no account. We count only anonymous local feature events (month-priced, gap-checked, link-copied, reset) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no sub counts, Bits totals, or income figures are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Common questions

Does a subscription bought on mobile pay me less because of Apple or Google's cut?

No, as of Twitch's October 2024 pricing change. Twitch charges more for a mobile subscription specifically to cover the app store's in-app-purchase fee, so your payout per sub is the same whether the viewer bought it on desktop or in the iOS/Android app. Enter your web tier price here either way — see the worked explainer.

Why is the revenue split 50% for some streamers and 60% or 70% for others?

Everyone starts at 50% of subscription revenue. Affiliates and Partners who sustain 100 Plus Points for three consecutive months move to 60% under Twitch's Plus Program, and those who reach 300 Plus Points move to 70%. Plus Points come only from paid recurring subs — 1 point per Tier 1, 2 per Tier 2, 6 per Tier 3; gifted and Prime subs earn none. This is the one number that actually changes your payout per sub — read your own current split off your Twitch dashboard rather than assuming one.

Why don't Bits follow the same split as subs?

A cheered Bit is worth a flat $0.01 to the streamer no matter what the viewer paid for the Bits bundle or what the streamer's subscription split is — Twitch's own cut is already built into what a viewer pays for Bits before the streamer ever sees the cheer. So Bits income is not reduced by a 50% or 70% split the way sub revenue is.

Does this tool estimate ad revenue?

No. Twitch publishes no standard ad CPM a static calculator could model honestly, and ad payouts vary by campaign and channel. Enter any ad revenue, sponsorship, or other income as the single "other monthly income" figure instead — this tool only computes the parts with documented, deterministic mechanics: subs and Bits.

Does anything about my numbers get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server and there is no account. Your inputs and target are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

vs-tracking-payouts-in-a-spreadsheet.htm.text:
← Twitch payout calculator

This calculator vs. tracking Twitch payouts in a spreadsheet

Names no specific product or company — this compares a free calculator against the generic method most streamers already use: a personal spreadsheet with a payout formula typed in once and copied down for every month.

QuestionSpreadsheet formulaThis calculator
Revenue split over a careerA constant typed in once, easy to leave at 50% after qualifying for the Plus Program's 60% or 70%A field you update the month your split changes, so a new split never silently underprices old-formula months
Whether a mobile subscription pays lessOften modeled as a fee reduction, following the outdated app-store-cut assumptionModeled as no difference, matching Twitch's current mobile pricing policy — see the linked explainer
Bits vs. sub-revenue splitEasy to accidentally apply the same split percentage to Bits as to subsBits are kept separate and always priced at a flat $0.01 each, never split
Whole-month income-goal checkA second sheet or a manual sum, often not kept in sync with the tier tabBuilt in — see total payout against your monthly target and how many more Tier 1 subs close the gap
History across months and seasonsIts actual strength — a running log month over monthPrices one month at a time; does not replace an income log
Shareable single scenarioRequires sending the whole file or a screenshotOne link, via "Copy shareable link," with no file attached

Neither tool sets your revenue split, your sub counts, or your Bits total — both are arithmetic on numbers you already have, and both are only as accurate as the figures you type in.

Common questions

Why not just track Twitch payouts in a spreadsheet?

Plenty of streamers do, and a spreadsheet is a fine tool for a monthly income log. The failure mode is not the spreadsheet itself — it is that your revenue split is not a constant across a career. It changes the day you qualify for Partner Plus, and a formula copied down a column keeps using whatever split was true the month you typed it, silently understating income every month after the split changes.

Does this calculator replace my income-tracking spreadsheet?

Not necessarily. This tool prices one month at a time and does not save a running history across months the way a spreadsheet's rows do. Many streamers use both: this calculator to get one month's split-and-Bits arithmetic right whenever their split or sub counts change, and their own spreadsheet to log the result alongside every other month for the year.
